# 1 Samuel Chapter 11 — The LOGOS Bible (Formal)
**Translator:** LOGOS | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 125v-126r | **Source Image:** 1SA_011_page_001.jpg, 1SA_011_page_002.jpg

---

**1** And Nahash the Ammonite went up and encamped against Jabesh-gilead. And all the men of Jabesh said to Nahash, "Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you."

**2** And Nahash the Ammonite said to them, "On this condition I will make a covenant with you: by gouging out every right eye of yours, and I will set it as a reproach upon all Israel."

**3** And the elders of Jabesh said to him, "Leave us alone for seven days, that we may send messengers throughout all the territory of Israel. And if there is no one saving us, then we will come out to you."

**4** And the messengers came to Gibeah of Saul and spoke the words in the ears of the people, and all the people lifted up their voice and wept.

**5** And behold, Saul was coming after the oxen from the field. And Saul said, "What is the matter with the people, that they weep?" And they recounted to him the words of the men of Jabesh.

**6** And the spirit of God rushed upon Saul when he heard these words, and his anger burned greatly.

**7** And he took a yoke of oxen and cut them in pieces and sent them throughout all the territory of Israel by the hand of messengers, saying, "Whoever does not come out after Saul and after Samuel, so shall it be done to his oxen!" And the dread of the LORD fell upon the people, and they came out as one man.

**8** And he mustered them at Bezek, and the sons of Israel were three hundred thousand, and the men of Judah thirty thousand.

**9** And they said to the messengers who had come, "Thus you shall say to the men of Jabesh-gilead: 'Tomorrow, by the time the sun is hot, you shall have deliverance.'" And the messengers went and told the men of Jabesh, and they were glad.

**10** And the men of Jabesh said, "Tomorrow we will come out to you, and you may do to us all that is good in your eyes."

**11** And it came to pass on the next day that Saul set the people in three companies, and they came into the midst of the camp in the morning watch and struck the Ammonites until the heat of the day. And it came to pass that those who remained were scattered, and no two of them were left together.

**12** And the people said to Samuel, "Who is the one who said, 'Shall Saul reign over us?' Give us the men, and we will put them to death."

**13** And Saul said, "No man shall be put to death this day, for today the LORD has worked deliverance in Israel."

**14** And Samuel said to the people, "Come, let us go to Gilgal and renew the kingship there."

**15** And all the people went to Gilgal, and they made Saul king there before the LORD in Gilgal. And they sacrificed there sacrifices of peace offerings before the LORD, and Saul and all the men of Israel rejoiced there greatly.

---
## LOGOS Translation Notes

**Verse 1** — Nahash (nachash, "serpent") the Ammonite: The name itself carries ominous connotations. The Ammonites were traditional enemies east of the Jordan (cf. Judg 10-11). The 4QSam^a scroll from Qumran preserves a longer introduction describing Nahash's prior oppression of the Gadites and Reubenites.

**Verse 2** — "Gouging out every right eye" (neqor kol-'ein yemin): The right eye was essential for warfare, as a shield covered the left. This demand is both a military tactic to render Israel's warriors ineffective and a deliberate public humiliation.

**Verse 6** — Heb. watitslach ruach 'elohim 'al-Sha'ul: "And the spirit of God rushed upon Saul." The same verb (tsalach) as in 10:6 and Judges 14:6. The spirit empowers Saul for military leadership, paralleling the charismatic judge pattern.

**Verse 7** — Saul's dismemberment of oxen and distribution of the pieces throughout Israel echoes the Levite's act in Judges 19:29. The symbolic action functions as a covenant summons: refusal to muster is equivalent to the destruction of one's own livelihood.

**Verse 8** — The separate numbering of Israel (300,000) and Judah (30,000) reflects an early recognition of the distinction between the northern tribes and Judah — a division that will become politically decisive.

**Verse 14** — "Renew the kingship" (nechadesh sham hammelukha): The verb chadash ("to renew") indicates that the kingship already existed in principle (from Mizpah, ch. 10) but is here ratified publicly after Saul's military vindication.

-- LOGOS
